meta.description: Butter-making template data for the Butter Builder wizard

cow.name: Cow Cream
cow.yield_notes: 1 pint heavy cream yields ~1 cup (8 oz) butter
cow.notes: Most common and versatile. Use heavy cream (36%+) for best yield.

goat.name: Goat Cream
goat.yield_notes: Lower yield than cow cream. Naturally homogenized - may need to collect cream over several milkings.
goat.notes: Naturally white (no beta-carotene). Tangier flavor. Harder to separate cream from milk - use a cream separator or let raw milk sit 24-48 hours.

sheep.name: Sheep Cream
sheep.yield_notes: Highest fat content of common dairy animals. Excellent yield per pint.
sheep.notes: Very rich with high fat. Makes incredibly flavorful butter. Seasonal availability (spring/summer).

buffalo.name: Water Buffalo Cream
buffalo.yield_notes: Very high fat content. Exceptional yield.
buffalo.notes: Traditional for Indian makhan and ghee. Very white, exceptionally creamy. Higher melting point than cow butter.

yak.name: Yak Cream
yak.yield_notes: High fat, excellent yield. Traditional in Tibetan and Nepali cuisine.
yak.notes: Used in po cha (Tibetan butter tea). Strong, distinctive flavor. Naturally golden-yellow.

sweet_cream.name: Sweet Cream Butter
sweet_cream.description: Classic fresh butter churned from sweet (uncultured) cream. The most common homemade butter.
tips: Cream should be 55-60°F (13-16°C) for best churning
Over-churning past separation makes butter greasy
Wash butter 3-4 times until water runs clear
Thorough washing removes buttermilk and extends shelf life

cultured.name: Cultured Butter
cultured.description: European-style butter made from cream fermented with live cultures. Tangier, more complex flavor with higher butterfat.
tips: Add 2 tbsp buttermilk or yogurt per pint of cream as starter
Culture at 70-75°F (21-24°C) until thick and tangy
Longer culturing = more tangy flavor
This is how most European butter is made (French, Danish, Irish)

compound.name: Compound Butter
compound.description: Finished butter mixed with herbs, spices, garlic, citrus, or other flavorings. A restaurant staple.
tips: Butter should be room temp but not melted when mixing
Finely mince all add-ins for even distribution
Roll into a log for easy slicing
Make multiple flavor rolls and freeze for later

ghee.name: Ghee (Clarified Butter)
ghee.description: Butter cooked until water evaporates and milk solids brown and settle. Nutty flavor, very high smoke point. Sacred in Ayurvedic tradition.
ghee.shelf_life: 3 months at room temp, 1 year refrigerated
tips: Use unsalted butter for cleaner flavor
Low and slow - rushing causes burning
Golden-brown solids = nutty ghee; dark brown = bitter
Strain through cheesecloth or coffee filter
Traditional Indian ghee uses cultured butter (desi ghee)

browned.name: Brown Butter (Beurre Noisette)
browned.description: Butter cooked until milk solids toast to a golden-brown, creating a nutty, caramelized flavor. French kitchen essential.
key_steps: Swirl and watch for color change
tips: Use a light-colored pan so you can see the color change
Swirl constantly - it goes from brown to burnt in seconds
The foam will subside when water has evaporated
Smells like toasted hazelnuts when ready

whipped.name: Whipped Butter
whipped.description: Butter whipped with air (or sometimes milk/cream) for a lighter, more spreadable texture straight from the fridge.
tips: Room temperature butter whips best
Add 1-2 tbsp cream per stick for extra lightness
Don't over-whip or it will become greasy
Great for spreading - uses less butter per slice

smen.name: Smen (North African Aged Butter)
smen.description: Moroccan/North African fermented and aged butter with a pungent, cheese-like flavor. Used in couscous, tagines, and special occasions.
tips: Traditional herbs: oregano, thyme, dried lavender
Must be completely airtight to age properly
Aged smen develops blue cheese-like flavor
Start with 1-month aging for milder flavor
Prized possession - families age smen for decades

butter_tea.name: Po Cha (Tibetan Butter Tea Butter)
butter_tea.description: Butter specifically prepared for Tibetan butter tea - churned from whole milk or cream, often from yak or dri (female yak).
key_steps: Churn fresh cream or whole milk
Do not wash extensively (some buttermilk adds flavor)
Churn butter and salt into tea
tips: Traditional pu-erh or black tea is best
Add salt - this is a savory drink, not sweet
Churn tea and butter together with a chandong (traditional churn)
Essential nutrition at high altitude - the fat provides energy and warmth
Yak butter is traditional but cow butter works

items.name: Cajun Spice
items.pairs_with: Corn on the cob, seafood, rice

basic_sweet_cream.title: Basic Sweet Cream Butter

instructions.text: Pour cold heavy cream into a large bowl or stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment. You can also use a food processor or mason jar.

Whip on medium-high speed. Cream will go through stages: soft peaks, stiff peaks, then grainy/curdled. Keep going. After 8-12 minutes, the butterfat will suddenly separate from the buttermilk with a splash.
Pour off the buttermilk through a fine strainer (save it for baking!). Squeeze the butter mass to expel more liquid.
Add ice water to the butter and knead/fold it to wash out remaining buttermilk. Pour off cloudy water. Repeat 3-4 times until water runs clear.
Knead in salt if desired. Shape into a block, log, or press into a butter mold. Wrap tightly in parchment or wax paper.
Refrigerate to firm up. Yields approximately 1 cup (8 oz / 225g) butter plus about 1 cup buttermilk.

notes: Save the buttermilk! Use it for pancakes, biscuits, salad dressings, or as a cultured cream starter.
Cream temperature matters: too cold and it takes forever; too warm and butter is soft and greasy. 55-60°F is ideal.
Mason jar method: fill jar 1/3 full, shake vigorously 15-20 minutes. Great arm workout!

basic_cultured.title: Cultured European-Style Butter

ingredients.item: live-culture buttermilk or plain yogurt (as starter)

instructions.text: Combine heavy cream and buttermilk/yogurt in a clean jar. Stir well. Cover loosely with cheesecloth or a coffee filter secured with a rubber band.
Let sit at room temperature (70-75°F / 21-24°C) for 24-48 hours. Cream will thicken and develop a pleasant tangy aroma. Longer = tangier.
Refrigerate cultured cream for at least 2 hours (overnight is best). Cold cream churns better.
Churn the cultured cream using a stand mixer, food processor, or mason jar until butter separates from buttermilk (8-15 minutes).
Strain off the cultured buttermilk (this is real, live-culture buttermilk - liquid gold for baking). Squeeze butter to expel more.
Wash butter with ice water 3-4 times until water runs clear. Knead in salt if desired.
Shape and wrap. This butter has a more complex, tangy flavor than sweet cream butter and higher butterfat content.

basic_cultured.yield: ~8 oz butter + ~1 cup true cultured buttermilk
notes: This is how butter is made in France, Denmark, and Ireland. The culture adds complexity and tang.
The cultured buttermilk byproduct is far superior to store-bought buttermilk for baking.
For stronger culture flavor, let cream ferment up to 72 hours.
Save 2 tbsp of the cultured buttermilk to start your next batch - perpetual culture!

basic_ghee.title: Traditional Ghee

instructions.text: Place butter in a heavy-bottomed saucepan over medium-low heat. Melt completely without stirring.
Once melted, reduce heat to low. The butter will begin to foam as water evaporates. Do not stir.
After 15-20 minutes, the foam will subside. You'll see clear golden liquid with milk solids settling to the bottom.
Continue cooking on low until milk solids turn golden-brown and the ghee has a nutty aroma (another 5-10 minutes). Watch carefully - it can burn quickly.
Remove from heat immediately when solids are golden (not dark brown). Let cool 5 minutes.
Strain through cheesecloth or a fine coffee filter into a clean, dry glass jar. Discard the browned solids.
Cool completely. Ghee will solidify to a golden-yellow semi-solid at room temperature. Store sealed.

notes: Ghee has a very high smoke point (485°F/252°C) - excellent for frying and searing.
Removing milk solids makes ghee suitable for many who are lactose intolerant or casein sensitive.
Traditional desi ghee starts from cultured (fermented) cream butter for deeper flavor.
In Ayurvedic tradition, ghee is considered a sacred food that promotes health and longevity.
Store at room temperature for up to 3 months, refrigerated up to 1 year.

basic_compound.title: Classic Compound Butter

instructions.text: Allow butter to soften at room temperature for 30-45 minutes. It should be pliable but not melted or greasy.
Finely mince, grate, or chop all add-in ingredients. Pat dry any fresh herbs or moist ingredients.
Place softened butter in a bowl. Add all flavoring ingredients. Mix thoroughly with a fork or spatula until evenly distributed.
Taste and adjust seasoning. Season with salt and pepper if needed.
Spoon butter onto a sheet of parchment paper or plastic wrap. Roll into a log shape, twisting ends to seal.
Refrigerate at least 1 hour to firm up. Slice into rounds as needed. Freeze extra logs for up to 3 months.

notes: Keep a few compound butter logs in the freezer - instant flavor upgrade for any meal.
Slice frozen rounds directly onto hot steak, fish, or vegetables.
Mix and match flavors: the flavor additions section has ideas for every cuisine.
Compound butter also makes a beautiful homemade gift wrapped in parchment.

basic_browned.title: Brown Butter (Beurre Noisette)

instructions.text: Cut butter into pieces for even melting. Place in a light-colored saucepan or skillet over medium heat.
Butter will melt, then foam. Swirl the pan occasionally. The butter will begin to crackle as water evaporates.
Once the crackling stops, watch closely. Milk solids will start to turn golden on the bottom of the pan. Swirl constantly now.
When butter smells like toasted hazelnuts and solids are golden-amber (not dark brown), immediately remove from heat.
Pour into a heatproof bowl to stop cooking. Use immediately or store refrigerated.

notes: Brown butter goes from perfect to burnt in seconds - never walk away.
Use a light-colored pan so you can see the color change.
Brown butter transforms: pasta, cookies, cakes, vegetables, fish, rice.
The French call it beurre noisette (hazelnut butter) for its nutty aroma.
For beurre noir (black butter), cook slightly darker and add capers and vinegar - classic with skate fish.

basic_smen.title: Smen (Moroccan Aged Butter)

instructions.text: Melt butter over low heat. Skim off any foam. Pour through cheesecloth to remove milk solids (like making ghee).
While still liquid, knead in salt, oregano, and thyme until thoroughly combined.
Pack tightly into a sterilized glass jar or clay pot, pressing out all air pockets.
Seal jar completely. Traditional smen is packed in a clay pot sealed with plaster.
Store in a cool, dark place. Age for a minimum of 1 month. Traditional smen ages for months or even years.
Use sparingly - a small amount adds tremendous depth to couscous, tagines, and rfissa.

notes: Smen develops a strong, funky, cheese-like flavor with age. Start with 1-month aged for mild smen.
In Morocco, families age smen for decades. Smen aged for a daughter's wedding is a prized tradition.
Always use a clean, dry utensil to scoop smen - moisture introduces spoilage.
The flavor is similar to aged Parmesan or very ripe Brie - intense but deeply savory.
A tiny amount transforms couscous and tagine the way fish sauce transforms Thai food.

basic_butter_tea.title: Po Cha (Tibetan Butter Tea)

ingredients.item: strong black tea or pu-erh tea

instructions.text: Brew tea extra strong - use twice the normal amount of tea. Pu-erh or any robust black tea works. Steep 5-7 minutes.
Pour hot tea into a blender (or traditionally, a chandong - a narrow wooden churn). Add butter, salt, and milk if using.
Blend vigorously for 2-3 minutes until frothy and well-emulsified. The butter should be fully incorporated, not floating on top.
Pour into cups and serve immediately while hot. Sip slowly - it's meant to warm and sustain.

notes: This is NOT a sweet drink - it's savory and salty, more like a broth than a tea.
At high altitudes in Tibet and Nepal, butter tea provides essential calories, fat, and hydration.
Traditionally made with yak butter (dri butter from female yaks), which has a distinctive flavor.
Tibetans may drink 40-60 cups per day at high altitude.
The fat helps prevent chapped lips at high altitude and extreme cold.

basic_whipped.title: Whipped Butter

instructions.text: Allow butter to soften at room temperature for 30-45 minutes. It should be very soft but not melted.
Place butter in a bowl. Using an electric mixer or stand mixer with whisk attachment, whip on medium-high speed.
Whip for 3-5 minutes until butter is light, fluffy, and increased in volume. Add cream a little at a time if desired for extra lightness.
Season with salt if desired. Transfer to a serving container.
Refrigerate to set slightly, but serve at cool room temperature for best spreadability.

notes: Whipped butter is about 30-50% more volume than the same weight of stick butter.
Great for people who want to use less butter per serving - it spreads further.
Don't use whipped butter for baking - the air content changes ratios.
Add flavoring ingredients while whipping for a whipped compound butter.

Whip finished butter with air for lighter, spreadable texture
Slowly cook finished butter to remove water and milk solids
Clarify the cultured butter, add herbs, and age for weeks/months
Skip the culturing step - churn fresh cream directly
Cook the cultured butter to make desi ghee (traditional Indian)
Mix finished cultured butter with flavorings for complex compound butter
Stop cooking earlier - keep some moisture, use solids

Start from cultured cream butter for desi ghee tradition

churning: Temperature is everything: cream at 55-60°F (13-16°C) churns best
Stand mixer with whisk: medium-high, cover with towel to prevent splashing
Food processor: fastest method, 3-5 minutes pulse then run
Mason jar: fill 1/3 full, shake 15-20 min. Great with kids!
KitchenAid: use the splash guard or a towel when butter breaks
The 'break' happens suddenly - butterfat clumps and buttermilk splashes out
If cream won't churn, it may be too cold. Let it warm 5 minutes and try again
washing: Washing removes buttermilk proteins that cause butter to spoil quickly
Use ICE water - cold water keeps butter firm during washing
Knead and fold butter in the water, pour off cloudy water, repeat
Continue until wash water is completely clear (3-5 washes)
Unwashed butter spoils in days; well-washed butter keeps for weeks
Some traditional butters (like for butter tea) are intentionally not fully washed
storage: Wrap tightly in wax paper or parchment, then foil for freezing
Butter absorbs odors - keep away from strong-smelling foods
Salted butter keeps longer than unsalted (salt is a preservative)
A butter bell/crock keeps butter spreadable on the counter for ~30 days
Freeze butter for up to 6-8 months with no quality loss
Ghee stores at room temperature for months - no refrigeration needed
troubleshooting: Cream won't break? Too cold. Let it warm to 58-62°F
Butter is too soft? Cream was too warm. Chill and re-knead in ice water
Butter tastes sour? Buttermilk wasn't fully washed out
Butter is white not yellow? Normal for goat/buffalo milk. Cow butter yellows from beta-carotene in grass
Grainy texture? Over-churned past the break point. Knead smooth in ice water
Low yield? Cream fat content may be too low. Use heavy/double cream (36%+ fat)
history: Butter-making dates back at least 4,500 years to ancient Mesopotamia
Vikings and Celts buried butter in peat bogs to preserve it - 'bog butter' has been found still intact after centuries
In medieval Europe, butter was a luxury food taxed by the church during Lent
Ghee has been used in India for over 5,000 years - mentioned in the earliest Vedic texts
The word 'butter' comes from Greek 'boutyron' - possibly meaning 'cow cheese'
Before refrigeration, butter was heavily salted (5-10%) to prevent spoilage
